content: The Lanaʻi Hookbill, scientifically known as Dysmorodrepanis munroi, was a species of finch belonging to the family Fringillidae. This bird was endemic to the island of Lanaʻi in Hawaii, meaning it was found nowhere else in the world. The species was last observed in the Kaiholeua Valley and the Waiakeakua area of the island. Its extinction is attributed to habitat loss, primarily due to human activities. In 1913, C. Munro collected the only known specimen of this bird on the island of Lanaʻi. Since then, no additional specimens have been observed or collected. The single specimen is currently preserved in the Bishop Museum in Honolulu, Hawaii. Adult Lanaʻi Hookbills were described as having light gray plumage with a greenish tinge. Their underparts were paler, almost white. A light band was visible along the wing, and a distinct light marking was present above the eye. The bird’s mandibles were uniquely shaped, curving toward each other in such a way that only the tip of the lower mandible made contact with the upper mandible, leaving a gap in the middle. The bird measured approximately six inches in length, but its weight remains unknown as no measurements were ever recorded. The Lanaʻi Hookbill was observed only a few times, all between approximately 1912 and 1918. In 1989, it was confirmed to be a distinct species. Its diet remains largely unknown, as the birds were never seen feeding. However, stomach dissections revealed that they consumed native berries from the island. Based on the bird’s uniquely shaped bill and relatively weak jaw muscles, it has been hypothesized that it may have also fed on endemic land snails. The extinction of these snails, likely due to human intervention, may have contributed to the decline and eventual extinction of the Lanaʻi Hookbill. The first live sighting of the species occurred on February 22, 1913, when Munro collected the single known specimen in the Kaiholena Valley of Lanaʻi. Munro was the only person to have ever seen the species alive, and most of what is known about the bird comes from his book, The Birds of Hawaii (1960). After 1913, Munro reported seeing the bird again on March 16, 1916, in the Kaiholena Valley, and on August 12, 1918, in Waiakeakua. The 1918 sighting was the last recorded observation of the species. By that time, much of the native akoko forest on Lanaʻi had been replaced by pineapple plantations, further contributing to the bird’s decline. The Lanaʻi Hookbill (Dysmorodrepanis munroi) was officially listed as extinct on the IUCN Red List in 1996.
